q: Wednesday evening club race on the lake. Ashore, Grey's crew tells you that Red crossed her on port far too close on the first beat; you were two legs away and saw nothing. You want to protest Red yourself. Can you?
a: No — for a Part 2 incident only a boat that was involved in it or saw it may protest; Grey herself can
o: Yes — any boat in the race may protest any other boat for any rule she hears about
Yes, but only as a joint protest signed by you and Grey together
Only if the race committee countersigns your protest form
why: Rule 60.4(a)(2): a boat's protest about a Part 2 or rule 31 breach is invalid unless she was involved in or saw the incident.

fig.title: Ashore after the race
lines: Red crossed Grey on port, first beat
You were two legs away, saw nothing
Grey's crew tells you at the bar

q: ILCA 7 nationals, 6 knots. After the race Blue's helm tells you that Grey pumped her mainsail all the way down the last run; you did not see it yourself. Can you protest Grey under rule 42, and what must you do?
a: Yes — the "involved or saw" limit applies only to Part 2 and rule 31; but since you did not see it, you must inform Grey at the first reasonable opportunity
o: No — only the jury on the water may protest a boat under rule 42
No — a boat may protest a rule 42 breach only if she was involved in or saw the pumping
Yes, and nothing more is needed: a written protest within the time limit is enough
why: Rule 60.4(a)(2) limits only Part 2 and 31 protests; rule 60.2(b)(3): incident not seen in the racing area — inform her at the first reasonable opportunity.

fig.title: After the race
lines: Blue says Grey pumped down the run

q: Dragon regatta in Split. After the finish the helm of 4471 screams abuse at the mark-boat crew and throws a winch handle at them. You write a protest against 4471 under rule 69 and lodge it. What happens to it?
a: It is invalid — an alleged rule 69 breach cannot be protested; your report goes to the protest committee, which decides whether to open a rule 69 hearing
o: It is heard as an ordinary protest and 4471 is disqualified from the race if the facts are proven
It is valid only if you hailed "Protest" at the moment of the incident
It is valid only if the race committee co-signs it, since race officials were the victims
why: Rules 60.4(a)(3) and 69.1(c): a report of misconduct is not a protest; the protest committee decides whether to act under rule 69.

fig.title: After the finish
lines: Throws a winch handle at them
You lodge a protest citing rule 69

q: You request redress, writing that the committee boat dragged after the preparatory signal; in the form you also mention that Blue, next to you, was over the line and never returned. The race committee then protests Blue using only your form. Is its protest valid?
a: No — a committee protest based on information from a request for redress is invalid
o: Yes — the race committee may protest any boat on any information it receives
Yes, provided Blue is informed before the protest time limit expires
No — a race committee may never protest a boat for a starting error; it only scores her OCS
why: Rule 60.4(b)(1): a protest by a committee based on information from a request for redress is invalid.

fig.title: Race office
lines: RC protests Blue on that alone

q: 29er Europeans. The race officer on the windward mark boat sees Grey hit the mark and sail on without taking a turn. The race committee wants to protest her. What must it do?
a: Inform Grey of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit — a notice on the official notice board is enough — and lodge a written protest in time
o: Hail "Protest" at Grey from the mark boat and hoist a red flag
Score Grey DSQ for the race without a hearing, as it would for OCS
Nothing — a committee may protest only breaches of the sailing instructions, not rule 31
why: Rules 60.1, 60.2(a)(2) and 60.2(d): a committee informs the boat after the race within the protest time limit, e.g. by a notice on the official board.

q: Before the medal race at a Palma regatta the technical committee measures your 470 jib and finds its luff 4 cm over the class maximum. What may the technical committee do?
a: Protest your boat — it has inspected the equipment and decided it does not comply with the class rules
o: Nothing — only another competitor may protest a class-rule breach
Disqualify you on the spot, without any hearing
Ask the race committee to protest, since a technical committee cannot
why: Rules 60.1 and 60.4(c)(3): the technical committee may protest after it has inspected and found non-compliance with class rules or rule 50.

q: In a hearing between you and Red about a leeward-mark incident, the evidence shows that Green — outside, not protested, present as a witness — forced Red down onto you. Can the protest committee penalise Green in this hearing?
a: Not in this hearing — it must close it, protest Green itself, then hear both protests together with Green as a party
o: Yes — any boat shown by the evidence to have broken a rule can be penalised at once
No — a boat not named in the original protest can never be penalised for that incident
Yes, but only if you or Red amend your protest form to name Green
why: Rules 60.4(c)(2), 60.5(b) and 63.2(d): a boat is penalised only as a party; the PC protests her, closes the hearing and hears both protests together.

fig.note: Three boats overlapped entering the zone

q: At the dock after a club race you tell the race officer loudly that Blue tacked right in front of you at the windward mark and that you protest her. Then you go home. Has a protest been made?
a: No — a protest must be in writing, identifying the protestor, the protestee and the incident, and be delivered to the race office within the time limit
o: Yes — telling the race officer within the protest time limit is enough at club level
Yes — your hail on the water was already the protest; the dock conversation only confirmed it
No — only the race officer may write a protest form, and he did not
why: Rule 60.3(a)–(b): a protest is written, identifies protestor, protestee and incident, and is delivered to the race office within the protest time limit.

fig.title: At the dock
lines: You tell the race officer about Blue

q: Saronic Gulf, J/24 fleet (hull 7.2 m). Blue, on port, crosses too close and you bear away to avoid her. You hail "Protest" at once but never show a red flag, and lodge the form in time. Is the protest valid?
a: No — a boat with a hull longer than 6 m must also display a red flag at the first reasonable opportunity
o: Yes — the hail at the first reasonable opportunity is enough for any boat
Yes — the flag is needed only when the other boat does not acknowledge the hail
No — the protest also needed a second hail at the finishing line
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): hail "Protest" and, if the hull is longer than 6 m, display a red flag at the first reasonable opportunity, until no longer racing.

fig.note: J/24, hull 7.2 m — you hailed, no flag

q: ILCA 7 club race on the river. Red, on port, forces you to bear away sharply. You hail "Protest" immediately but have no flag aboard; your written protest is lodged in time. Valid?
a: Yes — a boat with a hull under 6 m needs only the hail; no red flag is required
o: No — every boat must display a red flag; carry one on the boom
No — a single-hander must instead report the incident to the race committee at the finish
Yes, but only because Red answered your hail
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the red flag is required only when the protesting boat's hull length is more than 6 m.

q: 36-ft cruiser-racer, Bodrum. After a mark-room incident you hail and hoist a red flag within seconds. Two legs later the crew takes the flag down because it fouls the runner. You finish and lodge a protest. Valid?
a: No — the red flag must stay displayed until you are no longer racing, i.e. until you have finished and cleared the line
o: Yes — the flag only needs to be shown at the first reasonable opportunity, however briefly
Yes — a flag shown for a full leg satisfies the rule
No — but only because a 36-footer must display two flags, one on each shroud
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the flag is displayed until the boat is no longer racing (definition Racing: finished and cleared the line and marks).

lines: Hail and red flag within seconds
Flag taken down two legs later

q: Windward mark, 25 knots. Grey, tacking inside you, hits your 470 and you capsize. After righting and bailing, about three minutes later, you hail "Protest" towards Grey, who is now far away, and lodge a protest in time; no damage. Grey says the hail came too late. Validity?
a: Valid if the PC finds that three minutes after a capsize was the first reasonable opportunity; Grey, beyond hailing distance, only had to be informed then
o: Invalid — the hail must come within a few seconds of the incident in every case, whatever happened to the boat
Invalid — a hail that the other boat could not hear counts for nothing, so you should have sailed after Grey
Valid only because there was contact; after contact no hail is needed at all, whenever it comes
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1) and (b)(1): "first reasonable opportunity" is a question of fact; a boat beyond hailing distance is informed at that first opportunity.

fig.title: Windward mark, 25 knots
lines: Righted and bailed in about 3 min
Then you hail; Grey is far off

q: Trapezoid course, Melges 24 nationals. Black, the windward boat, touches your boom on the first reach; nothing is said. On the last beat, having thought it over, you hail "Protest" at Black and show a red flag. Valid?
a: No — the hail and the flag came nowhere near the first reasonable opportunity after the incident
o: Yes — any time before finishing counts as a reasonable opportunity
Yes — contact with the boom replaces the need for a timely hail
No — Black had to be hailed by her sail number, not just "Protest"
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the hail and the flag must come at the first reasonable opportunity after the incident, not legs later.

fig.title: Melges 24 nationals
lines: Black touches your boom, first reach
Hail and flag on the last beat

q: On the run you see Yellow, in your fleet about 300 m ahead, hit the offset mark and sail on without a turn. She cannot possibly hear you. What do you have to do to protest her?
a: Inform Yellow at the first reasonable opportunity — hail her when you next come close, or tell her at the dock — then lodge a written protest in time
o: Hail "Protest" loudly at the moment you see it; nothing else is needed
Nothing on the water — a boat that hits a mark is penalised by the race committee without a hearing
You cannot protest — only boats within two hull lengths of the mark may protest a touch
why: Rule 60.2(b)(1): when the protestee is beyond hailing distance, the protestor need only inform her at the first reasonable opportunity.

lines: She is 300 m ahead, out of earshot

q: You watch Blue, five lengths ahead of you, leave the offset mark to starboard when the sailing instructions require port, and carry on down the run. Do you need to hail "Protest" and show a flag?
a: No — when the incident was a failure to sail the course, you need only inform Blue of your intention to protest at the first reasonable opportunity
o: Yes — hail "Protest" and display the red flag at once, as for any incident in the racing area
No — rounding errors can be protested only by the race committee
No — nothing at all is needed before the written protest, since there was no contact
why: Rule 60.2(b)(2): when the incident was a failure to sail the course, the only requirement is to inform the protestee at the first reasonable opportunity.

q: Star fleet. Red, on port, hits your bow: pulpit bent, a hole in the topsides. In the chaos nobody hailed or showed a flag. You lodge a protest within the time limit. Valid?
a: Yes — with injury or serious damage from the incident no hail or flag is required, but you must try to inform Red within the protest time limit
o: No — the hail and the flag are required in every case for a boat over 6 m, however bad the damage
Yes, but only because the race committee saw the collision and can confirm it to the hearing
No — a boat with serious damage must retire and request redress instead of protesting
why: Rule 60.2(c): with injury or serious damage from the incident, 60.2(a) and (b) do not apply; the protestor tries to inform the other boat within the time limit.

lines: Red on port hits your bow
Pulpit bent, hole in the topsides
No hail, no flag from anyone

q: At the gybe mark Grey's boom hits your crew, who goes overboard. You stop, recover him and sail in; no hail, no flag. Later you lodge a protest. Grey objects that there was no flag — both boats are 8 m long. Is the protest valid?
a: Yes — when it was clear a crew member was in danger, the hail and flag are not required; you need only try to inform Grey within the protest time limit
o: No — once the crew was back aboard you had to hoist the flag and hail, and continue racing to keep the protest alive
No — a boat that stops racing to recover her crew loses the right to protest over that incident
Yes, but only if the race committee or a rescue boat witnessed the man overboard
why: Rule 60.2(c): when a crew member is in danger, rules 60.2(a) and (b) do not apply; the protestor tries to inform the other boat within the protest time limit.

fig.title: Gybe mark
lines: Grey's boom hits your crew — overboard

q: Hobie 16 club race. Blue barges in at the committee boat and you shout "Hey, no room, you're out!" Later you lodge a protest; Blue says you never hailed "Protest". Was your shout enough?
a: No — the rule requires the hail "Protest"; shouting about the incident is not a protest hail
o: Yes — any hail that makes clear you object to her action is enough
Yes — at the start no hail at all is needed, since rule 18 does not apply
No — only a hail of the other boat's sail number counts
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the protesting boat shall hail "Protest" at the first reasonable opportunity.

fig.note: Blue barges in at the committee boat

q: Dragon (8.9 m), Lake Garda. Grey fails to give you room at the breakwater. Your crew hoists the red flag at once, but nobody hails; Grey clearly saw the flag. Is your protest valid?
a: No — the hail "Protest" is required as well as the flag; the flag alone does not satisfy the rule
o: Yes — a boat over 6 m may choose either the hail or the flag
Yes — seeing the flag is as good as hearing a hail
No — because the flag should have been shown only after finishing
why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): both the hail at the first reasonable opportunity and, for hulls over 6 m, the red flag are required.

fig.title: Breakwater
lines: Grey gives no room at the obstruction

q: You finish last. On the VHF channel given in the sailing instructions the race committee calls: "Sail 17, we intend to protest you under rule 42 for the last run." Is that a proper notification?
a: Yes — a committee informs the boat of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit; it does not hail or fly a flag
o: No — the committee had to hail "Protest" and show a red flag on the committee boat at the time
No — a race committee cannot protest under rule 42; only an Appendix P jury can
Yes, but only if it is repeated in writing on the notice board before you reach the shore
why: Rule 60.2(a)(2): a committee protestor informs the boat of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit.

fig.title: After your finish
lines: RC on the SI radio channel

q: After a port–starboard incident near the pin, both you and Red hail "Protest" at each other and both lodge protest forms. Will there be two separate hearings?
a: Normally one — the protest committee may combine hearings about the same incident into a single hearing with both boats as parties
o: Two — each protest must be heard separately, in the order lodged
One — the protest lodged second is automatically invalid
None — when both boats protest each other, the protests cancel out
why: Rule 63.2(b): the PC may combine hearings about the same or closely connected incidents (never with a rule 69 hearing).

fig.title: Race office
lines: You protest Red; Red protests you

q: A rescue boat reports to the jury that during race 3 a boat was holed in a collision that nobody protested. Can the jury protest the boat it believes was at fault, and what must it do first?
a: Yes — a protest committee may protest a boat when it learns of an incident with possible injury or serious damage; it informs her at the first reasonable opportunity
o: No — a protest committee may only hear protests lodged by others; it can never lodge one itself
Yes, but only if it hails "Protest" and shows a red flag from the jury boat before the boat finishes
No — without a protest from one of the boats involved, the incident is closed once the time limit passes
why: Rules 60.4(c)(1) and 60.2(b)(4): the PC may protest on learning of possible injury or serious damage; it informs the boat at the first reasonable opportunity.

q: The sailing instructions say nothing about a protest time limit. The last boat finishes at 15:40. You deliver your protest form to the race office at 17:50. In time?
a: No — the default time limit is two hours after the last boat finishes, i.e. 17:40
o: Yes — the default limit is two hours after your own finish, whatever the others do
Yes — without a limit in the SI, protests may be lodged until the end of the day
No — the limit is 30 minutes after the committee boat docks
why: Rule 60.3(b)(1): the default protest time limit is two hours after the last boat finishes the race, unless the SI say otherwise.

fig.title: Protest time limit
lines: SI silent on the time limit

q: Sailing instructions: "Protest time limit: 60 minutes after the committee boat docks." The last boat finished at 14:00, the committee boat docked at 14:30 and you lodge your protest at 15:45. Valid?
a: No — the sailing instructions' limit applies: 60 minutes after docking, i.e. 15:30
o: Yes — the rulebook's two hours after the last finish (16:00) always overrides the SI
Yes — the two limits add up, so you had until 16:30
No — but only because the limit is counted from your own finish
why: Rule 60.3(b): when the sailing instructions state a different protest time limit, that limit applies.

fig.title: Protest time limit
lines: SI: 60 min after the RC boat docks

q: Your protest form names Blue and describes the leeward-mark incident, where and when — but you left the "rules alleged to have been broken" box empty. Blue asks the protest committee to declare it invalid. Will it?
a: No — a written protest must identify the protestor, the protestee and the incident; naming a rule is not required for validity
o: Yes — a protest that cites no rule number is invalid
Yes, unless you fill in the rule before the hearing starts
No, but the committee may then consider only the rules you name orally at the hearing
why: Rule 60.3(a): a protest is written and identifies the protestor, the protestee and the incident; no rule need be cited.

q: Protest time limit 17:00. At 16:00 you hand your completed form to the bar manager and go for a shower; it reaches the race office at 17:30. Valid?
a: No — the protest must reach the race office (or follow the method in the SI) within the time limit; handing it to someone else is not delivery
o: Yes — handing it to any club employee within the time limit stops the clock
Yes — the time you signed the form is what counts, not the time it arrived
No — it should have been handed to the protestee rather than to the race office
why: Rule 60.3(b): a protest is delivered to the race office, or by another method stated in the SI, within the protest time limit.

fig.title: Protest time limit 17:00
lines: Form handed to the bar manager 16:00
SI: deliver to the race office

q: Your protest arrives 25 minutes after the time limit because you stood by a dismasted Yellow and towed her into harbour. Yellow's helm is not the protestee. What can the protest committee do?
a: It may extend the time limit if there is good reason — helping a boat in trouble is a classic good reason — and hear the protest
o: Nothing — the protest is automatically invalid; the time limit can never be extended
It must hear it — the time limit never applies to a boat that gave help
It must declare it invalid but award you redress instead
why: Rule 60.3(b): the protest time limit applies unless the protest committee decides there is good reason to extend it.

q: Next morning, in the photographer's gallery, you spot Grey's crew hiking with his torso outboard of the lifelines for a whole leg of yesterday's race 4. Race 4's protest time limit expired yesterday. Can you still protest?
a: Yes — the limit is then two hours after the information became available to you, and you must inform Grey at the first reasonable opportunity
o: No — the time limit for race 4 ran out two hours after the last finisher yesterday, whatever you find later
No — only the technical committee may protest equipment or crew matters found from photographs
Yes — a protest based on photographs has no time limit at all and needs no notice to Grey
why: Rule 60.3(b)(2): for other protests the limit is two hours after the information became available; rule 60.2(b)(3): inform the protestee.

fig.title: Next morning
lines: Grey's crew outboard of the lifelines

q: The sailing instructions forbid using the engine inside the race area. At 13:00, in the lunch break between race 2 (finished 12:00) and race 3 (started 14:30), Grey is seen motoring through the course. The protest committee finds a breach. To which race is her penalty applied?
a: Race 2 — a penalty for a breach when not racing is applied to the race sailed nearest in time to the incident
o: Both races 2 and 3
Race 3 — penalties always apply to the next race sailed
No race — a boat cannot be penalised for anything done when she is not racing
why: Rule 60.5(c): if a boat broke a rule when not racing, her penalty applies to the race sailed nearest in time to the incident.

fig.title: Lunch break
lines: SI: no engine in the race area

q: The jury protests you after the safety boat reported that you "holed" Red in a collision. At the hearing it turns out there was only a scratch in Red's gelcoat and no injury. What happens?
a: The hearing is closed — a protest committee's own protest about a reported collision proceeds only if there was injury or serious damage
o: The hearing continues as an ordinary Part 2 protest between you and Red
You are disqualified anyway — a protest committee's protest is always valid
The hearing is converted into a request for redress for Red
why: Rule 63.4(a)(2): a hearing on a PC protest under 60.4(c)(1) is closed when there was no injury or serious damage.

q: Blue protests you citing rule 10. The protest committee finds that both boats were on starboard and that you, clear astern, hit her transom — a breach of rule 12, which the form never mentions. Can it disqualify you?
a: Yes — when the committee decides a boat broke a rule, it disqualifies her whether or not that rule was mentioned in the protest
o: No — a boat can be penalised only under the rule written on the protest form
No — the protest must be dismissed and Blue may lodge a new one citing rule 12
Yes, but only with a lesser penalty than disqualification, since the rule was not cited
why: Rule 60.5(c): the PC disqualifies a boat it finds broke a rule, whether or not the applicable rule was mentioned in the protest.

fig.title: Hearing
lines: You, clear astern, hit her transom

q: You touched Red at the gybe mark as the windward boat, no damage, and did two turns straight away. Red still protests. The committee finds you broke rule 11. What is the outcome for you?
a: No further penalty — you already took the applicable penalty for that breach
o: Disqualification — the turns do not count once a protest has been lodged
A 20 % scoring penalty on top of the turns
Disqualification, unless Red agrees to withdraw her protest
why: Rule 60.5(c)(2): a boat that has already taken the applicable penalty is not penalised further (unless the penalty is a non-excludable DSQ).

fig.title: Gybe mark
lines: You, windward, touch Red — no damage

q: On port you hit Grey hard: her pulpit is torn off and the forestay fitting cracked. You take a Two-Turns Penalty and finish third. Grey protests. What should the committee decide about your penalty?
a: Disqualify you — with serious damage the applicable penalty was to retire, so the turns were not an applicable penalty
o: Nothing further — a Two-Turns Penalty always closes a Part 2 incident
Add a 20 % scoring penalty to your third place
Order you to pay for the repair instead of a scoring penalty
why: Rule 44.1(b): with serious damage the penalty is to retire; rule 60.5(c)(2) protects only a boat that took the applicable penalty.

fig.title: Port–starboard
lines: Pulpit torn off, forestay fitting cracked
You did two turns, finished third

q: You protest Blue under rule 11. The committee finds that you, the leeward boat, luffed suddenly without giving her room to keep clear (rule 16.1) and that Blue kept clear. What can happen to you?
a: You can be disqualified — the committee may penalise any party to the hearing, including the protestor, for a rule it finds was broken
o: Nothing — the protestor cannot be penalised in her own protest
Nothing — the committee may only rule on the rule the protest cites
Only a warning — a protestor is at most warned
why: Rule 60.5(b)(1) and (c): a boat may be penalised as a party to a hearing, whether or not the rule was mentioned in the protest.

fig.note: You, leeward, luffed sharply; Blue kept clear

q: At a week-long championship the committee finds your keel 3 mm outside class tolerance and disqualifies you from race 1; you are sure the measurement was wrong. Can you sail race 2 tomorrow with the boat unchanged?
a: Yes, if you state in writing that you intend to appeal — but if you do not appeal or lose it, you are disqualified without a hearing from all later races you sailed
o: No — after a class-rule DSQ the boat may not race until the fault is corrected, appeal or not
Yes — a DSQ applies to one race only and has no effect on later races
Yes, but only with the written consent of every other competitor
why: Rule 60.5(d)(4): a boat may race on unchanged after declaring in writing an appeal; if she loses or does not appeal, DSQ without a hearing for those races.

q: A rival protests your J/70 for a mast step 6 mm out of the class position. The committee finds the deviation was caused by a grounding last month and gives no advantage in speed. What does it decide?
a: No penalty — the deviation came from damage and gave no advantage — but you may not race again until it is fixed, unless that is not reasonably possible
o: Disqualification from the race — a class rule is a class rule, whatever caused the deviation
Disqualification from the whole series, as for any measurement breach found during an event
No penalty and no further action — damage is always a complete excuse for a class-rule breach
why: Rule 60.5(d)(1)–(2): no penalty when the deviation is from damage or wear and gives no performance gain; the boat must be fixed before racing again.

fig.title: Class-rule hearing
lines: Mast step 6 mm out of position

q: The sailing instructions mark rule 55 (trash disposal) as [DP]. A bottle slipped overboard from your cockpit during the race; within the protest time limit you report it yourself to the jury. What happens next?
a: The protest committee decides on an appropriate discretionary penalty, taking into account the evidence it finds relevant — no hearing is required
o: A full hearing must be held, with you as protestor and protestee
You are disqualified from the race without a hearing, as for a black-flag start
Nothing — a boat cannot be penalised for a breach she reports herself
why: Rule 64: when a boat reports within the protest time limit that she broke a DP rule, the PC decides the penalty; no hearing is required.

fig.title: Self-report
lines: You report it to the jury in time

q: You are disqualified in race 3 after losing a port–starboard protest. The series of seven races has one discard. May you discard the DSQ?
a: Yes — a disqualification from a protest hearing is excludable unless the rule broken prescribes a non-excludable one (rule 2, rule 69)
o: No — any disqualification counts in the series total and cannot be discarded
No — only DNF, DNC and OCS scores may be discarded under the Low Point System
Yes, but only if the protest committee expressly says so in its written decision
why: Rule 90.3(b) and A2.1: the worst score is excluded unless it is a non-excludable DSQ (DNE); an ordinary DSQ is excludable.

fig.title: Series of seven, one discard
lines: Race 3: DSQ after a rule 10 protest

q: At the start the committee boat dragged its anchor downwind, swinging the line. At the signal you were behind the line as laid, but the race committee, sighting from its new position, scored you OCS. Do you have grounds for redress?
a: Yes — an improper action or omission of the race committee that made your score significantly worse through no fault of your own
o: No — a boat is always responsible for judging the starting line herself, whatever the committee boat does
No — redress is available only for injury or physical damage, not for starting errors
Yes, but only if at least two other boats were affected by the same error
why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): redress for a score made significantly worse, through no fault of the boat, by an improper action or omission of a committee.

q: Leading the second beat, you see a sailor from another fleet in the water, separated from her capsized Optimist and not moving. You stop, pull her aboard and hand her to a rescue boat, then finish 14th. Redress?
a: Yes — giving help to a person in danger under rule 1.1 is a ground for redress when it made your score significantly worse
o: No — helping other fleets is voluntary and carries no compensation
No — redress for help given applies only when a rescue boat was not available
Yes, but only as a first place, since you were leading
why: Rule 61.4(b)(4): redress for a score made significantly worse by giving help under rule 1.1 (not to the boat herself or her crew).

lines: Sailor in the water, not moving
You stop and pull her aboard
Hand her to a rescue boat

q: Red, on port, holes your bow at the windward mark. She takes a Two-Turns Penalty and sails on; you retire to stop the leak. Is redress available to you?
a: Yes — physical damage caused by a boat breaking a Part 2 rule that took a penalty or was penalised is a ground for redress
o: No — redress is never given for incidents between boats; that is what protests are for
No — because Red took her penalty, the matter is closed
Yes, but only if you also win a protest against Red
why: Rule 61.4(b)(2): injury or physical damage because of the action of a boat that broke a Part 2 rule and took a penalty or was penalised.

fig.note: Red holes your bow, takes two turns

q: Grey, on port, forces you to crash-tack to avoid her and you lose five places; no contact, no damage. Grey takes two turns. You want your five places back through redress. Will you get them?
a: No — losing places because of another boat's breach, without injury or physical damage, is not a ground for redress
o: Yes — any loss of places caused by a boat breaking a Part 2 rule is a ground for redress
Yes, provided Grey's turns were taken too late
No — because Grey took her penalty; otherwise redress would be due
why: Rule 61.4(b)(2) requires injury or physical damage from the other boat's breach; places lost without damage are not a ground.

fig.title: First beat
lines: Grey on port forces you to crash-tack

q: Lake race, 5 knots dying to nothing. You were leading by 200 m when the breeze shut off on your side; the fleet sailed round you in a new breeze and you finished 12th. Redress?
a: No — the weather is not a ground for redress; your score was not worsened by anything listed in the rule
o: Yes — losing the lead through no fault of your own is exactly what redress is for
Yes — the race committee should have abandoned, so its omission is a ground
No — but only because you did not request it before finishing
why: Rule 61.4(b) lists the grounds for redress; a wind shift or dying breeze is none of them, and abandoning is the RC's discretion.

fig.title: Dying breeze
lines: Wind shuts off on your side

q: At the leeward mark your spinnaker halyard jams, the kite goes in the water and you drop from 3rd to 15th. Nobody else was involved. You request redress for the places lost. Outcome?
a: The request is refused — your score got worse through your own boat's fault, and no listed ground applies
o: Redress granted — average points, since the gear failure was not deliberate
Redress granted — equipment failure is an "improper omission" by the boat
The request is refused only because you did not retire
why: Rule 61.4(b): redress needs a score made worse through no fault of the boat and one of the listed grounds; a gear failure is neither.

fig.title: Leeward mark
lines: Halyard jams, kite in the water

q: On the first reach a harbour ferry, not racing and required to keep clear of you, alters towards you and hits your quarter, bending the rudder stock. You limp in last. Is this a ground for redress?
a: Yes — physical damage caused by a vessel not racing that was required to keep clear is a ground for redress
o: No — incidents with commercial traffic are outside the racing rules
No — only damage caused by another racing boat counts
Yes, but only if the race committee abandons the race
why: Rule 61.4(b)(3): injury or physical damage because of a vessel not racing that was required to keep clear or found at fault under IRPCAS or government rules.

fig.title: First reach
lines: Hits your quarter, rudder stock bent
Ferry was required to keep clear

q: You lose a protest hearing in which you were a party and are disqualified. You think the committee got the rules wrong. You lodge a request for redress against its decision. What will the committee do with it?
a: Refuse it — a protest committee decision in a hearing where the boat was a party is expressly not a ground for redress; the remedy is an appeal
o: Hear it — an improper action of any committee is a ground for redress
Hear it, but only with a differently composed protest committee
Refuse it — redress is never available against a protest committee for any reason
why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): improper action or omission of a committee, but not a PC decision when the boat was a party; appeal under rule 70 instead.

fig.title: After the hearing
lines: You were a party, got DSQ
You think the rules were misapplied
You request redress against the PC

q: Your rudder is damaged by a port-tack boat at 11:30; you retire and reach the shore at 12:00. The last boat finishes at 12:30; the protest time limit is 14:30. By when must your request for redress be delivered?
a: By 14:30 — within the protest time limit, or two hours after the incident, whichever is later
o: By 13:30 — two hours after the incident, which is all the rule allows
By 12:30 — before the last boat finishes
Any time during the regatta — requests for redress have no time limit
why: Rule 61.2(b)(1): a request based on a racing-area incident is delivered within the protest time limit or two hours after the incident, whichever is later.

q: Last day of the series. At 16:10 the protest committee posts a decision in a hearing you were not party to, which moves you from 3rd to 5th overall. You want redress. By when must you request it?
a: Within 30 minutes after the decision was posted — by 16:40
o: Within two hours of the posting — by 18:10
Within 24 hours, as for a request to reopen a hearing
You cannot — a decision in a hearing you were not party to cannot be challenged
why: Rule 61.2(b)(2): a request based on a protest committee decision on the last scheduled day of racing is delivered no later than 30 minutes after it was posted.

q: You catch the principal race officer on the dock and say: "You finished me in the wrong place — I want redress." He nods. Have you requested redress?
a: No — a request for redress must be in writing, stating the reason for it, and be delivered to the race office within the time limit
o: Yes — a verbal request to the race officer within the time limit is sufficient
Yes — since the race officer agreed, no written request is needed
No — redress can be requested only by the race committee on your behalf
why: Rule 61.2(a)–(b): a request for redress is written, states the reason, and is delivered to the race office (or as the SI say) in time.

fig.title: On the dock
lines: You tell the PRO you want redress

q: You get redress for race 4 of a six-race series (you were scored OCS by the race committee's error). Your other scores are 3, 5, 2, 4 and 6. What is the usual way the committee will score race 4?
a: Usually the average of your other races to a tenth — here 4.0 — or another fair arrangement such as your place at the time of the incident
o: First place — the boat wronged by the committee always gets the best available score
The same points as the boat that finished just ahead of you at the time of the incident
Redress always means abandoning race 4 for the whole fleet and resailing it
why: Rule 61.4(c) and A9: the fairest arrangement, e.g. average points of the other races (to a tenth) or the place at the time of the incident.

q: Blue, out of contention, deliberately sails you into the committee boat at the finish to help her team-mate win the series; you finish 9th. The protest committee penalises Blue under rule 2 with a DNE. Can you have your own score corrected?
a: Yes — a score made significantly worse by the action of a boat that was penalised under rule 2 (or rule 69) is a ground for redress
o: No — Blue's DNE is the end of the matter; redress is only for committee errors
No — there was no physical damage, so no redress
Only if Blue's team-mate is also disqualified
why: Rule 61.4(b)(5): redress when the score was worsened by an action of another boat (or her crew or support person) that led to a rule 2 or rule 69 penalty.

fig.title: Finishing line
lines: Blue deliberately pushes you into the RC boat

q: Reviewing its finishing video in the evening, the race committee realises it recorded Yellow as DNF although she finished 6th; the protest time limit has passed and Yellow has gone home. What can the race committee do?
a: Correct its own error from its records, or request redress for Yellow itself — a race committee may request redress for a boat
o: Nothing — only Yellow may request redress, and the time limit has passed
Nothing — once posted, results may be changed only by the protest committee after a hearing
Score Yellow 6th only if all other boats agree in writing
why: Rule 90.3(c): the RC corrects a scoring error from its records; rule 61.1(b): the race committee may request redress for a boat.

fig.title: Evening, race office
lines: Time limit passed, Yellow gone home

q: Red is awarded redress and given 2.5 points for race 3 after being scored DNF by a committee error. You finished 3rd in that race and ask whether your score now drops to 4th. Does it?
a: No — when redress is given by adjusting a boat's points, the other boats' scores stay as they are unless the committee decides otherwise
o: Yes — every boat that finished behind the redressed boat moves down one place
Yes — Red's 2.5 points push every boat with 3 or more points down a place
No — but only because 2.5 points is not a whole place in the results
why: Rule A6.2: when the PC adjusts a boat's points as redress, the scores of the other boats are not changed unless the PC decides otherwise.

q: Your own crew falls overboard on the run; you stop, recover him and finish 20th instead of about 5th. You request redress citing rule 1.1 (helping a person in danger). Will it be granted?
a: No — help given to your own boat or your own crew is expressly excluded as a ground for redress
o: Yes — recovering a person in danger is always a ground for redress
Yes — but only average points of the other races
No — because you should have left him to the rescue boat
why: Rule 61.4(b)(4): redress for giving help under rule 1.1 — but not to the boat herself or her own crew.

q: You are the protestee in a hearing. The chairman opens by asking the protestor when she hailed, whether she showed a flag and when the form was delivered, before anyone describes the incident. Why?
a: Because the protest committee must first decide whether the protest is valid; if it is not, the hearing is closed
o: Because the protestor always speaks first about everything, including the facts
Because the committee wants to check whether you agree with the protestor's account
Because validity is checked only at the end, so the chairman is getting it out of the way early
why: Rule 63.4(a): the protest committee first takes evidence and decides validity; an invalid protest or request means the hearing is closed.

q: Grey was notified of the time and place of the hearing but does not turn up; her skipper is seen at the bar. You, the protestor, are present. What may the protest committee do?
a: Proceed with the hearing in Grey's absence, taking your evidence and deciding the protest
o: Nothing — a hearing cannot be held unless all parties are present
Disqualify Grey immediately for failing to attend, without taking evidence
Postpone the hearing until Grey chooses to attend
why: Rule 63.1(b): when a party fails to attend after being notified, the protest committee may nevertheless decide the protest or request.

fig.title: Hearing time
lines: Grey notified of time and place

q: After a rule 18 protest, the owner of Red, who watched from the club terrace, wants to represent Red at the hearing instead of the helmsman who was steering. May he?
a: Normally not — in a Part 2, 3 or 4 protest the representative must have been on board at the time, unless the committee decides otherwise for good reason
o: Yes — the owner may always represent his boat in any hearing, whether or not he was aboard
Yes — provided the helmsman signs a written authorisation naming the owner as representative
No — a boat may be represented only by the person who was steering at the time, never anyone else
why: Rule 63.1(a)(4): for Part 2, 3 or 4 protests the representative shall have been on board at the time of the incident, unless the PC decides otherwise.

fig.title: Rule 18 protest
lines: Red's owner watched from the terrace

q: One of the three protest committee members is the coach of Blue, the boat you protested. He says nothing about it. What should happen?
a: He must declare it; he may sit only if all parties agree or the committee finds the conflict not significant — object as soon as you know
o: Nothing — a coach is not a party to the hearing, so there is no conflict of interest
The hearing must be cancelled and the protest dismissed because of the conflict
He may sit and take part as long as he does not vote on the final decision
why: Rule 63.3: a member declares any possible conflict of interest; a party objects as soon as possible; he sits only if all consent or it is not significant.

q: You bring the helm of Green as a witness to your protest against Red. He wants to sit in the room for the whole hearing so as to understand the case. May he?
o: Yes — witnesses may attend the whole hearing if the protestor agrees
Yes — at club level witnesses are treated like parties
No — a witness from another boat may give evidence only in writing
a: No — a witness who is not a party or a committee member is excluded except while giving his evidence
why: Rule 63.4(e): a witness is excluded from the hearing except when giving evidence, unless he is also a party or a member of the protest committee.

fig.title: Your witness
lines: Wants to stay for the whole hearing

q: Your bowman was the only person on your 36-footer with a clear view of the port-tack boat at the moment of the incident. Can he give evidence in your protest hearing?
a: Yes — a party may call witnesses, and a crew member is an ordinary witness whose evidence the committee weighs like any other
o: No — crew members of a party boat count as parties and may not testify as witnesses
No — only people from boats not involved in the incident may be witnesses
Yes, but only in writing, since he was aboard a boat that is a party to the hearing
why: Rule 63.4(b): the committee takes the evidence of the parties present and of their witnesses; a crew member may be a witness.

fig.title: Your witness
lines: Bowman had the only clear view

q: At the hearing Red's helm says: "The mark-boat driver told me afterwards that you were clearly inside the zone." You object that this is hearsay. What does the committee do with it?
a: It may admit it — hearsay is admissible — and decides how much weight to give it; it may also exclude evidence it finds irrelevant
o: It must exclude it — hearsay is never admissible in a protest hearing
It must accept it as proven fact, since it comes from a race official
It must adjourn and summon the mark-boat driver before continuing
why: Rule 63.4(b): hearsay evidence is admissible, but the PC may exclude evidence it considers irrelevant or unduly repetitive, and weighs it under 63.5(a).

q: Blue's witness states that you were two lengths from the mark when the overlap was broken. You want to ask him how far away he was and what he was doing at the time. May you?
a: Yes — a party present at the hearing may question anyone who gives evidence
o: No — only committee members may question witnesses
No — a party may question only the other party, not her witnesses
Yes, but only through written questions handed to the chairman
why: Rule 63.4(c): a party present at the hearing may question any person who gives evidence.

fig.title: Hearing
lines: Blue's witness: "two lengths from the mark"

q: A member of the protest committee was on the windward mark boat and saw the incident between you and Grey. What must he do at the hearing?
a: State that he saw the incident, as soon as reasonably possible, in the presence of the parties; he may then give his evidence like a witness
o: Withdraw from the committee at once — a member who saw the incident may not take part
Say nothing and simply vote according to what he saw
Give his evidence privately to the other members after the parties have left
why: Rule 63.4(d): a committee member who saw the incident shall, as soon as reasonably possible, state that fact in the presence of the parties.

fig.title: Protest committee
lines: One member was on the mark boat

q: You and Red give flatly contradictory accounts of who tacked first at the port lay line; there are no witnesses. Red says the committee must dismiss the protest because nothing is proven beyond doubt. Is she right?
a: No — the committee finds facts on the balance of probabilities, deciding which account it finds more likely
o: Yes — a boat may be penalised only when the facts are proven beyond reasonable doubt
Yes — with no witnesses a protest between two boats must always fail
No — the committee must accept the protestor's account whenever there is a conflict
why: Rule 63.5(a): the PC weighs the evidence and finds the facts on the balance of probabilities (unless the rule applied requires otherwise).

fig.title: Hearing
lines: Who tacked first at the lay line?

q: A four-member protest committee splits two to two on whether you broke rule 17. How is the decision made?
a: By a simple majority — and when the vote is tied, the chairman of the hearing may cast an additional vote
o: A tie means the protest fails and no boat is penalised
A tie means the protest must be reheard by a new committee
The decision must be unanimous, so the committee keeps deliberating
why: Rule 63.5(b): decisions are by simple majority; when votes are equal, the person in charge of the hearing may cast an additional vote.

q: The notice of race says a breach of the restricted-area rule carries a 10 % scoring penalty; the sailing instructions say disqualification. You broke it. Which does the committee apply?
a: The rule it believes will provide the fairest result for all boats affected — the conflict between the NoR and SI is resolved that way
o: The sailing instructions — the later document always prevails over the notice of race
The notice of race — the earlier document always prevails over the sailing instructions
Neither — when two event documents conflict no penalty can be imposed at all
why: Rule 63.5(c): when rules in the NoR, SI or other event documents conflict, the PC applies the rule it believes gives the fairest result for all boats affected.

q: The committee tells you orally that you are disqualified and why. You want the facts found, the rules applied and the reasoning on paper to decide about an appeal. What are you entitled to?
a: The information in writing, provided promptly, if you request it in writing within seven days of being informed of the decision
o: Nothing further — decisions are given orally only, unless an international jury sits
A written decision only if you pay a fee set by the organising authority
A written decision only if you announce the appeal first
why: Rule 63.6(a)–(b): the parties are informed promptly; on a written request within seven days the PC gives the information in writing.

q: Half an hour before the hearing you and Grey talk it through, agree you were both partly wrong and shake hands. You ask the committee to drop your protest. Can it?
a: Yes — the committee may allow a protest to be withdrawn; otherwise it must hear every protest lodged
o: No — once lodged, a protest must always be heard to the end
Yes — but only if Grey takes a Two-Turns Penalty ashore
No — only the race committee can withdraw a protest
why: Rule 63.2(a): the protest committee shall hear all protests and requests delivered, unless it allows one to be withdrawn.

q: You are told at the door that your hearing starts in two minutes; nobody has shown you the protest form against you. What are you entitled to before the hearing proceeds?
a: To be told the time and place, to see the protest, and to have reasonable time to prepare — ask for it before the hearing proceeds
o: Nothing — the committee sets its own timetable and parties attend when called
To refuse to attend, in which case the protest is dismissed
To have the hearing postponed to the next day in all cases
why: Rule 63.1(a): parties are notified of the time and place, given access to the protest, and allowed reasonable time to prepare.

fig.title: At the jury room door
lines: You have not seen the protest

q: Red brings a 40-minute GoPro video from her stern and insists the committee watch all of it, plus a friend's drone footage of other races. The committee watches two minutes around the incident and declines the rest. Did it act correctly?
a: Yes — the committee takes the evidence it considers necessary and may exclude evidence it finds irrelevant or unduly repetitive
o: No — a party has the right to have all her evidence viewed in full
No — video evidence must either be viewed completely or excluded completely
Yes — but only because video is never admissible in a protest hearing
why: Rule 63.4(b): the PC takes the evidence it considers necessary and may exclude evidence it considers irrelevant or unduly repetitive.

fig.title: Hearing
lines: PC watches two minutes around the incident

q: You lost a hearing at 18:00 on Tuesday. On Wednesday morning the fleet's tracking data is published and shows you were clearly outside the zone, contradicting the facts found. What can you do, and by when?
a: Request that the hearing be reopened on new significant evidence — in writing, within 24 hours of being informed of the decision
o: Nothing — once the facts are found they cannot be challenged in any way
Lodge a fresh protest against the same boat for the same incident
Appeal to the national authority on the facts within 24 hours
why: Rule 63.7(a)(3) and (b): a party requests a reopening in writing within 24 hours of being informed of the decision; new significant evidence is a ground.

fig.title: Wednesday morning
lines: Tracking shows you outside the zone

q: On the last scheduled day of racing the committee informs you of its decision at 15:05. You believe it made a significant error. By when must you request a reopening?
a: Within 30 minutes of being informed — by 15:35
o: Within 24 hours — by 15:05 tomorrow
Within the protest time limit of the previous day
Any time before the prize-giving
why: Rule 63.7(b)(2): on the last scheduled day a request to reopen is delivered within 30 minutes after the party was informed of the decision that day.

fig.title: Last day of racing
lines: You believe there was a significant error

q: The committee agrees to reopen your hearing because it may have made a significant error in applying rule 18.3. Who should sit on the reopened hearing?
a: If practicable, a committee that includes at least one member who was not on the original committee
o: Exactly the same members as the original hearing, nobody else
An entirely new committee with none of the original members
Only the chairman of the original hearing, sitting alone
why: Rule 63.7(c): for a significant error, if practicable at least one new member; for new evidence only, if practicable a majority of the original members.

q: The committee found as a fact that you were overlapped inside Grey at the zone, and penalised Grey. Grey wants to appeal on the ground that the overlap did not exist. Can she?
a: No — a party may appeal the committee's decision or its procedures, but not the facts it found
o: Yes — any party may appeal on any point, including the facts
Yes — facts can be appealed if a witness signs a statement
No — appeals exist only for the protestor, never for the protestee
why: Rule 70.1: a party may appeal a protest committee's decision or its procedures, but not the facts found.

q: You disagree with how a club protest committee applied rule 20 to your case and want to appeal. To whom is the appeal made?
a: To the national authority of the organising club, following the procedure in Appendix R
o: To the race committee of the event, which reviews protest committee decisions
To World Sailing directly, bypassing the national authority
To the commodore of the organising club, as the senior officer
why: Rules 70.1 and 70.5: a party appeals to the national authority; appeals must conform to Appendix R.

q: At an international regatta with an international jury properly constituted under Appendix N, the jury disqualifies you. You want to appeal to your national authority. Can you?
a: No — decisions of a properly constituted international jury cannot be appealed
o: Yes — every protest committee decision may be appealed to the national authority
Yes, but only to World Sailing rather than to the national authority
No — but only because foreign competitors may never appeal
why: Rule 70.3(a): there is no appeal from the decisions of an international jury constituted in compliance with Appendix N.

q: The sailing instructions of a club series state: "Decisions of the protest committee are final; there is no appeal." The club has not obtained approval from the national authority for this. Does the clause bind you?
a: No — the right of appeal may be denied under rule 70.3 only in the listed cases, with the national authority's approval where it requires it, and stated in the NoR or SI
o: Yes — the sailing instructions may change any rule, including rule 70
Yes — at club level there is never a right of appeal anyway
No — because the right of appeal can only be removed by the race committee, not the SI
why: Rule 70.3: appeals may be denied only for the cases listed, several needing national authority approval, and only when stated in the NoR or SI.

q: In the boat park after racing, the helm of 1192 punches a competitor who beat him on the last run. You saw it. What is the correct route under the rules?
a: Report it to the protest committee — this is possible misconduct under rule 69, handled in a rule 69 hearing, not a protest
o: Lodge a protest under rule 2 within the protest time limit
Hail "Protest" at him and lodge a Part 2 protest form
Nothing — events ashore after racing are outside the racing rules
why: Rule 69.1: a competitor shall not commit misconduct; reports are dealt with under rule 69 and are not grounds for a protest (69.1(c)).

q: The sailing instructions forbid support boats inside the course area while racing. Your coach drives his RIB through the fleet on the run to film you. The jury opens a hearing. Who can be penalised?
a: The coach, as a support person, may be warned or excluded — and your boat too may be penalised if it may have gained an advantage from his breach
o: Only your boat — a coach cannot be the subject of a protest committee hearing
Only the coach — a boat can never be penalised for something her support person did
Nobody — support boats are outside the jurisdiction of the protest committee entirely
why: Rule 62: the PC may hear a support person and warn or exclude him (62.3); under 62.4 the boat may also be penalised if she may have gained an advantage.

fig.title: Support person hearing
lines: Coach RIB inside the course while racing

q: Needing Blue to finish behind you for the series, you deliberately luff her into the committee boat at the finish, then do two turns. Blue protests. What penalty does the committee impose if it finds the collision was deliberate?
a: A disqualification that is not excludable — a clear breach of rule 2 (sportsmanship and fair sailing) carries a DNE, and the turns do not cure it
o: No further penalty — you already took a Two-Turns Penalty for the Part 2 breach
An ordinary disqualification, which you may discard
A 20 % scoring penalty, since Blue was not damaged
why: Rule 2: a boat penalised under rule 2 receives a disqualification that is not excludable; a deliberate breach is not cured by turns.

fig.note: You luff Blue into the committee boat on purpose

q: At the leeward mark you know you failed to give Grey mark-room; she says nothing, hails nothing, and nobody protests. What does the basic principle of sportsmanship expect of you?
a: To take the appropriate penalty promptly — or retire — even though no one protested
o: Nothing — without a protest there is no breach
To offer Grey a place in the results after the race
To wait for the committee to decide whether you broke a rule
why: Basic Principle, Sportsmanship and the Rules: a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes the appropriate penalty, which may be to retire.

q: Twelve boats are entered in a club series scored under the Low Point System. In race 2 you finish fourth. How many points do you score for that race?
a: 4 points — first place scores 1, second 2, and so on
o: 9 points — entries minus place plus one
0.75 points — the old Bonus Point System
3 points — fourth place minus one
why: Rule A4: under the Low Point System first place scores 1 point, second 2, third 3 and each place thereafter one more.

q: Twenty-three boats are entered in the regatta; eighteen started race 3. You retired with a broken boom and are scored DNF. How many points is that?
a: 24 points — the number of boats entered in the series plus one
o: 19 points — the number of starters plus one
23 points — the number of boats entered
18 points — last of the boats that started
why: Rule A5.2: a boat that did not start, sail the course or finish, retired or was disqualified scores the finishing place one more than the boats entered.

q: The notice of race says rule A5.3 applies. 40 boats are entered; 31 came to the starting area for race 5. Red did not come out at all; Grey came out but did not start. What do they score?
a: Red 41 points (entries plus one); Grey 32 points (boats in the starting area plus one)
o: Both 41 points — entries plus one, as in the default rule
Both 32 points — boats in the starting area plus one
Red 41 points; Grey 31 points — last of those present
why: Rule A5.3 (when the NoR or SI say so): a boat in the starting area scores boats in the starting area + 1; a boat that did not come scores entries + 1.

fig.title: Race 5, NoR: A5.3 applies
lines: Grey: came out, did not start (DNS)

q: Six races, one discard. Your scores are 2, 7, 3, 7, 1, 4. Which race is discarded?
a: Race 2 — with two equal worst scores, the one from the race sailed earlier is excluded
o: Race 4 — the later of the two equal worst scores
You choose which of the two sevens to drop
Both sevens — equal worst scores are discarded together
why: Rule A2.1: if a boat has two or more equal worst scores, the score(s) for the race(s) sailed earliest in the series are excluded.

q: After discards you and Blue are tied on 15 points. Your race scores are 1, 2, 6, 6 (discard 8); Blue's are 1, 1, 5, 8 (discard 9). Who places ahead and why?
a: Blue — listing each boat's counting scores best to worst, 1-1-5-8 beats 1-2-6-6 at the second score
o: You — your worst counting score, 6, is better than Blue's 8
Blue — because her discarded score is worse than yours
You — the boat with the best single race wins the tie
why: Rule A8.1: a series tie is broken by listing each boat's scores best to worst and comparing; the first difference decides. Excluded scores are not used.

q: You and Grey are tied in the series and your counting scores, listed best to worst, are identical: 1, 2, 3, 4. In the last race you were 4th and Grey 2nd; in the second-last race you were 1st, Grey 4th. Who finishes ahead?
a: Grey — with identical lists best to worst, the tie goes to the boat with the better score in the last race
o: You — the better score in the second-last race is what decides first
You — the boat with more first places in the series wins the tie
The tie stands and the prize for the place is shared between you
why: Rule A8.2: if a tie remains, the boats are ranked by their scores in the last race, then the next-to-last, and so on (excluded scores are used here).

q: You and Red cross the finishing line at exactly the same moment, contesting third place, and the race committee cannot separate you. How are you scored?
a: Both get 3.5 points — the points for third and fourth places are added together and divided equally
o: Both get 3 points — a dead heat gives both boats the better place
Both get 4 points — a dead heat gives both boats the worse place
The committee tosses a coin to decide who is third
why: Rule A7: boats tied at the finishing line share the points for the place they tie for and the following place(s), divided equally.

q: Black finished second in race 6 but is disqualified after a protest hearing. You finished fifth. What happens to your score?
a: You move up to fourth place — every boat with a worse finishing place than the disqualified boat moves up one place
o: Nothing — a disqualification never changes other boats' scores
You move up only if the protest committee says so in its decision
You move up two places, since Black's points are shared out
why: Rule A6.1: when a boat is disqualified, retires after finishing or is scored NSC, each boat with a worse finishing place moves up one place.

q: Flag Z was displayed. You were in the triangle in the last minute and received a 20 % penalty; the sailing instructions say nothing more about it. 34 boats are entered and you finished 3rd. What is your race score?
a: 10 points — 20 % of 35 (the DNF score) is 7, rounded to the nearest whole number, added to your third place
o: 3.6 points — your third place plus 20 % of your own score of 3
9.8 points — third place plus 6.8, with no rounding applied
35 points — a Z-flag penalty is scored the same as DNF
why: Rule 44.3(c) via A5.2: 20 % of the DNF score, rounded to the nearest whole number (0.5 upward), added to the place — but never worse than DNF.

fig.title: Flag Z start
lines: In the triangle in the last minute

q: The results sheet shows your sail number with "NSC" against race 2 — you had missed the offset mark and did not go back. What does NSC mean and how is it scored?
a: Did not sail the course — scored like DNF: boats entered plus one
o: Not scored, the race was abandoned for you — no points
No sail-number certificate — a measurement penalty
Did not start, corrected — scored as OCS
why: Rule A10 and A5.2: NSC means the boat did not sail the course; she scores points for the finishing place one more than the number of boats entered.

q: In a dying breeze only one boat, Yellow, finishes within the time limit; the other 20 are still a mile out. The race committee says it will abandon the race "since only one boat finished". Is that correct?
a: No — a race is scored if it is not abandoned and at least one boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit; the rest are DNF
o: Yes — a race needs at least three finishers within the time limit to be scored
Yes — a race needs at least half the fleet to finish within the time limit to be scored
No — but only because Yellow could request redress if the race were abandoned
why: Rule 90.3(a): a race is scored if not abandoned and at least one boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit, even if later RET or DSQ.

fig.title: Dying breeze
lines: Yellow finishes within the time limit

q: The posted results show you 11th in race 4, but the finishing sheet and the finish-boat video both put you 7th. The protest time limit has passed. What is the straightforward way to get this fixed?
a: Point it out to the race committee — it corrects an error it finds from its own records or observations without any hearing; if it refuses, request redress
o: Lodge a protest against the race committee within the protest time limit of the next race
Nothing can be done — results are final once posted
Lodge a protest against the boat scored 7th
why: Rule 90.3(c): the RC corrects a scoring error it finds from its own records or observations, with no hearing; a committee error is also a ground for redress.

q: The notice of race states that rule 90.3(e) applies. The regatta's last protest time limit ended Sunday at 15:00 and results were posted at 15:30. On Tuesday you notice a race committee adding error that cost you second overall. Can the results be changed?
a: No — under 90.3(e) results cannot be changed by actions started more than 24 hours after the last time limit, decision or posting, except under rules 6, 69 or 71
o: Yes — a race committee must correct its own scoring errors whenever they are found, at any time
Yes — the 24-hour rule applies only to protests and redress, not to scoring errors
No — results can never be changed after the prize-giving, whatever the notice of race says
why: Rule 90.3(e): when the NoR says so, no score changes from actions started over 24 h after the last time limit, decision or posting, except rules 6, 69, 71.

q: After a port–starboard incident Red suggests you both go to "arbitration" to avoid a full hearing. Neither the notice of race nor the sailing instructions mention Appendix T. Is arbitration available?
a: No — Appendix T (arbitration and the post-race penalty) applies only when the notice of race or sailing instructions say so
o: Yes — arbitration is always available for Part 2 protests under the racing rules
Yes — provided the jury has at least one international judge
No — arbitration exists only for rule 69 cases
why: Appendix T preamble: all or part of the appendix applies only if the notice of race or sailing instructions so state.

fig.title: After the incident
lines: NoR and SI silent on Appendix T

q: Appendix T applies at a J/24 nationals. You realise you broke rule 10 against Grey, who protested; no damage. Before the hearing starts you want to limit your loss. What can you do, and how much does it cost?
a: Take a Post-Race Penalty before the hearing begins — a 30 % scoring penalty, by a written statement to the arbitrator or a protest committee member
o: Take a 20 % scoring penalty by writing to the race committee before the hearing begins
Do two turns in the harbour before the hearing, which cancels the protest
Nothing — once a protest is lodged only the hearing can decide on any penalty
why: Rule T1: a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule or rule 31 may take a 30 % Post-Race Penalty at any time after the race but before the hearing starts.

q: At an arbitration meeting under Appendix T you want to bring your mastman, who saw the incident, to describe it to the arbitrator. May you?
a: No — at an arbitration meeting each party is represented by one person who was on board; witnesses are not permitted
o: Yes — each party may bring up to two witnesses to arbitration
Yes — but he may speak only after the arbitrator gives an opinion
No — but only because crew members can never testify in any proceeding
why: Rule T2: an arbitration meeting is held only if each party is represented by a person who was on board; witnesses are not permitted.

fig.title: Arbitration meeting
lines: You want to bring your mastman

q: At arbitration the arbitrator gives her opinion that the protest committee would probably find you broke rule 11 and disqualify you. Grey is the protestor. What are the possible next steps?
a: You may take the 30 % Post-Race Penalty; Grey may ask to withdraw her protest; if the protest is not withdrawn, a full hearing is held
o: The arbitrator's opinion is the decision — you are disqualified and the matter ends
You must accept the 30 % penalty; the protest is closed automatically
Grey must withdraw her protest once the arbitrator has spoken
why: Rules T3–T4: after the arbitrator's opinion a boat may take a Post-Race Penalty, a protestor may ask to withdraw; if not withdrawn, a hearing follows.

q: In a request for redress hearing about a race committee error, Red's helm says the protest committee itself should be treated as a party because it is "the other side". Who are the parties here?
a: Red, as the boat requesting redress, and the race committee as the body alleged to have acted improperly; a protest committee is never a party
o: Red and the protest committee, since the committee decides against one of them
Red alone — committees are never parties to any hearing under the rules
Every boat in the race, since redress may change all their scores
why: Definition Party: in a redress hearing, the boat requesting it and the body alleged to have made an improper action or omission; a PC is never a party.

q: Arguing in the bar, Grey's helm says: "Case 50 in the Case Book is a rule, so the protest committee is bound by it." Is he right about its status?
a: Not quite — the Case Book is World Sailing's authoritative interpretation of the rules, which a committee follows, but a case is not itself a rule
o: Yes — the cases are published by World Sailing and are rules like any other document in the rulebook
No — the Case Book is informal guidance that a protest committee may ignore as it pleases
No — only the Call Book for match racing has the status of a rule
why: Introduction and definition Rule: the Cases are World Sailing's authoritative interpretations; they are not listed among the documents that are rules.
